posts.title: Investor styles: 30 names, one set of questions
posts.summary: The plan for a series on how 30 well-known investors actually invest, the 14 questions every profile answers, and how the records will be graded and ranked.

posts.title: Global macro: a primer on trading currencies, interest rates and whole markets
posts.summary: Global macro traders bet on whole economies with borrowed money, and the part of their method that an individual can use is the free public data they watch to decide how much risk to carry.

posts.title: Stan Druckenmiller: big bets, small losses
posts.summary: Druckenmiller's results came less from being right than from betting large in liquid markets when conviction was high, cutting fast when wrong, and standing aside when cold; the famous 30% a year rests on press reports of his own firm's numbers, not on a public audited series.

posts.title: Ray Dalio: rules, many small bets, and a record in two halves
posts.summary: Ray Dalio built the largest hedge fund by writing his decisions down as testable rules and spreading risk over many unrelated bets, and the record shows the method worked very well until 2011, poorly from 2012 to 2024, and well again once the fund shrank.

posts.title: Value investing: a primer on buying businesses for less than they are worth
posts.summary: Value investing means buying a share of a business for well below a careful estimate of its worth, and the record shows the idea is sound while cheap stocks lagged for most of 2007 to 2025 and most stock pickers trail an index.

posts.title: Warren Buffett: patience, float and a record that changed after 1998
posts.summary: Buffett's 19.7% a year over 61 years is the best-documented record in investing, but it rests on cheap insurance money and permanent capital as much as on stock picking, nearly all of the lead over the index was built before 1999, and what an individual can take from it is the behaviour, not the structure.
